title: Triangle Midsegments
short: A midsegment is parallel to the third side and half as long.

blocks.html: A midsegment of a triangle joins the midpoints of two sides. Every triangle has three. With the midpoint formula from Distance and Midpoint Formulas and the parallel-line facts behind Triangle Sum and Exterior Angle Proofs, we can show that a midsegment always does two surprising things.

Put the triangle on a grid in a smart spot: $A(0, 0)$, $B(2a, 0)$ and $C(2b, 2c)$. (Using $2a$, $2b$, $2c$ keeps the midpoints free of fractions.) The midpoint of $\overline{AC}$ is $D(b, c)$ and the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$ is $E(a + b, c)$. $\overline{DE}$ is horizontal, just like $\overline{AB}$, so they are parallel. $DE = (a + b) - b = a$, while $AB = 2a$. Since the triangle was any triangle, this holds for all of them.

blocks.name: geoboard
blocks.cap: Drag the corners. The midsegment $\overline{DE}$ stays parallel to $\overline{AB}$, and its length is always half of $AB$.

blocks.html: Triangle Midsegment Theorem: a midsegment is parallel to the third side and half as long.

blocks.title: Finding lengths
blocks.q: $D$ and $E$ are the midpoints of $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$, and $BC = 26$. Find $DE$. If $DE$ were $9.5$, what would $BC$ be?
steps: Going the other way, the third side is twice the midsegment: $BC = 2 \cdot 9.5 = 19$.

blocks.title: With algebra
blocks.q: $\overline{DE}$ is a midsegment of $\triangle ABC$, parallel to $\overline{BC}$, with $DE = x + 4$ and $BC = 3x - 2$. Find $BC$.

blocks.title: Checking with coordinates
blocks.q: $A(2, 6)$, $B(0, 0)$ and $C(8, 2)$. $D$ and $E$ are the midpoints of $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$. Verify the theorem for $\overline{DE}$.
steps: Slopes: $\overline{DE}$ has $\frac{4 - 3}{5 - 1} = \frac{1}{4}$ and $\overline{BC}$ has $\frac{2 - 0}{8 - 0} = \frac{1}{4}$. Equal slopes: parallel.

blocks.html: Pairing a midsegment with the wrong side. The midsegment is parallel to (and half of) the side it does not touch. Joining the midpoints of $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ gives a segment parallel to $\overline{BC}$. Check: its endpoints sit on the two other sides.
